paragraphs.heading: Feedbacks in brief
paragraphs.text: A climate change feedback is a natural process that affects how far global temperatures rise for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions. A positive feedback amplifies the starting change, so in a warming world it adds to the warming, while a negative feedback weakens it. Calling a feedback positive or negative says nothing about whether it is good or bad.

paragraphs.heading: A physical feedback
paragraphs.text: Feedbacks can be split into physical ones and partly biological ones. Water vapor feedback is one of the physical kind, along with the loss of reflective snow and ice cover. Water vapor is a strong greenhouse gas in its own right. It also shapes feedbacks in how clouds and temperatures are spread through the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Warmer air holds more water
paragraphs.text: The feedback rests on the Clausius–Clapeyron relation, which says that saturation vapor pressure is higher in a warmer atmosphere. As the atmosphere heats up, the total amount of water vapor in it goes up. Because water vapor is a greenhouse gas, that extra vapor warms the air further. The warmer air can then hold even more water vapor, so the change keeps feeding itself.

paragraphs.heading: Another name for it
paragraphs.text: Scientists sometimes call it the specific humidity feedback. The reason is that relative humidity, written RH, stays almost constant over the oceans but falls over land. Land warms faster than the ocean does, and a drop in RH has been observed since the year 2000.

paragraphs.heading: Part of a bigger balance
paragraphs.text: Water vapor feedback works inside a larger set of feedbacks. Added together, all feedbacks still come to a negative total, mainly because a warmer planet gives off more heat radiation, but that total is becoming less negative as emissions go on. So warming is slower than it would be without feedbacks, yet it will speed up if emissions stay at current levels. Scientists estimate the strength of each feedback with global climate models, checked against observations whenever possible.
